summary: Research deliverable landed: docs/research/cloudflare-platform-limits.md, 943 lines with 31 distinct cited official Cloudflare URLs and 11 explicitly unverified items. It resolves open question Q5 and materially narrows Q2/Q3/Q4. Key facts now locked as decisions D8-D13 in STATE.md: Workers inbound body is capped by the ZONE plan (Free/Pro 100 MB) while a Worker isolate has only 128 MB memory, so large-file ingest must be chunked; R2 multipart state must live outside the Worker (Cloudflare states this explicitly), making the chunk-session schema a day-one D1 decision; R2 multipart needs >=5 MiB parts, <=10000 parts, <=5 GiB per part, <=4.995 TiB per object, and allows only 1 write/sec per key; R2 egress is free and an R2 object body can be returned as the Response body with no enforced size limit; presigned URLs expire in 1s-7d, cannot use custom domains, and are unrevocable bearer tokens; D1 is documented as auto-commit with db.batch() as the only atomic unit and no BEGIN/COMMIT/ROLLBACK anywhere; D1 replicas may be arbitrarily out of date unless withSession()/bookmark is used; only 6 concurrent in-flight connections are allowed per invocation, shared across fetch/R2/D1/KV/Queues/Cache; Cron gives 5 triggers per account on Free with minute granularity, UTC only, and no documented delivery guarantee.

Corrected an earlier inaccurate environment claim. STATE.md and AGENTS.md previously implied the machine had no usable web access. The accurate fact is narrower: the harness web_fetch tool is rejected because public hostnames resolve to the non-public TUN address 198.18.0.203. Ordinary HTTP works, and fetching the .md variant of a docs page with Invoke-WebRequest is a proven, reproducible path. Both files were corrected so a future session does not wrongly conclude that primary-source research is impossible here.

Research finding that invalidates part of the requested initialisation design: a running Worker cannot provision its own D1 database and R2 bucket and then bind to them, because bindings are deploy-time configuration and Cloudflare documents the D1 REST API as control-plane/administrative rather than a data-plane path. summary: The user was right and I was wrong: resources CAN be auto-provisioned at deploy time. I had asserted that D1 must be created beforehand and that database_id is required. Cloudflare documents an Automatic provisioning feature under which wrangler deploy creates KV, R2, D1 and others when the configuration declares a binding WITHOUT a resource id (and for R2, without a bucket name), naming them after the Worker. Behaviour differs by path: wrangler dev creates local resources that persist; wrangler deploy creates them and writes their ids back to the config file; but deploying from the dashboard (which is what Workers Builds does) creates the resources and does NOT write the ids back into the repository. wrangler.jsonc was rewritten accordingly to omit database_id and bucket_name. Recorded as decision D31.

Credential architecture specified by the user: only the key lives in the deployment secret, while each host address, port and credential is encrypted with that key and stored in D1, and arbitrary hosts plus their collection directory paths are added through the project front end. Implemented as: single SSH_MASTER_KEY secret; AES-GCM 256 via WebCrypto with a fresh random IV per encryption and the host id plus field name bound in as additional authenticated data; the API returns only a fingerprint, never a credential; hosts and source_rules tables added; global rules use a NULL host_id and per-host rules a host_id, unioned at collection time with exclusions evaluated first. Recorded as D32 and D33. An explicit honest limit is recorded rather than glossed over: an attacker holding both the D1 database and the master key can recover every credential.

summary: Prototype verdict: PASS. A deployed Worker connected to a real remote host over SSH and returned its bytes intact. Measured on the deployed Worker: ssh connect + auth 288-294 ms, sftp list /etc 202 ms (83 entries), sftp readFile 214 ms, WebCrypto sha256 under 1 ms, r2 put 217 ms; roughly 1.4 s end to end per file. Three files were checked against a hash computed independently ON THE HOST by sha256sum: /etc/hostname (24 bytes), /etc/alpine-release (7 bytes) and /etc/passwd (1226 bytes) all matched exactly, and the R2 objects were confirmed present with identical sizes. This closes the CPU-budget risk recorded as D24: the handshake uses about one hundredth of the paid plan ceiling, so the collection channel chosen in D14 is viable.

Bug found only against a real host, and the reason it could not be caught locally: Wrangler bundles without type checking, and edgeport AlgorithmPrefs.cipher is an ARRAY of algorithm names, but the code passed a bare string. The handshake therefore died at KEXINIT construction with TypeError names.join is not a function. Fixed by passing a preference list with AES-GCM first and aes-ctr as fallback; chacha20-poly1305 stays excluded because it would be pure JS. A list was chosen over a single pinned cipher so a host without GCM still works. The JSON error response now also carries a stack, because with no type checking in the build a dependency shape mistake can only surface at runtime and a stack turns that from guesswork into a line number.

summary: Registry integrity incident, self-reported. Two sessions were appending to this file concurrently and both drew event ids from the same counter, so e023 and e024 were defined twice with different content. Worse, the de-duplication pass that caught this resolved collisions by keeping whichever line came first and silently discarding the other, which deleted two genuine records - including the prototype verdict - from the ledger. Prevention recorded in FORMAT.md: a collision must abort the write, never resolve itself, and every write must be verified by unique-id count.

summary: Scale limits supplied by the user, answering Q7 and closing it: at most 50 devices (hosts), no single file larger than 100 MB, and total R2 usage must stay at or below 10 GB. The 100 MB per-file figure agrees with what event e014 already recorded ("single-file maximum size generally under 100 MB"), so that part is a confirmation rather than a change. The 10 GB ceiling is NEW and is a CAPACITY BUDGET, not merely a size limit: it implies the store must bound its own total bytes, which in turn requires a retention/eviction policy and a decision about whether superseded object versions stay in R2. Nothing in the schema or the code measures or enforces total stored bytes today. The 50-host figure bounds a full sweep and therefore the run/resume design, because D13 caps a single Cron invocation at 15 minutes of wall clock.

Grill round 4 answers. Q1 ACCEPTED: a cron sweep that works within a wall-clock budget and persists a cursor (which host, which path) into D1, resuming on the next invocation, with a target freshness of 15-30 minutes. Q2 REVISED BY THE USER, overriding the recommendation: old files are to be deleted automatically to stay inside the 10 GB budget, but files carrying an IMPORTANT mark are never deleted, and if the important-marked set alone fills the budget then no new files are synchronised at all. This introduces a requirement that did not exist before - a per-object importance/pin flag plus an eviction policy that must never delete a pinned object, and a capacity guard that refuses new work rather than evicting pins. Note the old policy of never deleting anything is now explicitly rejected. Q4 ACCEPTED: two tables, collection_runs plus collection_issues, to hold receipts including capacity refusals, which only become visible if they are persisted. Q3 PARTIALLY ANSWERED BUT CONFLICTS WITH A VERIFIED PLATFORM FACT: the user asked for a custom domain to serve presigned downloads with a 2-hour expiry and an optional share password, and D11 (research section 9.2, citing https://developers.cloudflare.com/r2/api/s3/presigned-urls/) states that presigned URLs work only on <ACCOUNT_ID>.r2.cloudflarestorage.com and CANNOT be used with custom domains, the documented alternative being a public bucket behind WAF HMAC validation (Pro plan or above). The requirement as stated is achievable, but only by the Worker issuing its own short-lived signed token and streaming the object, not by an R2 presigned URL. That reinterpretation is PROPOSED, not yet confirmed by the user. Also recorded: the user pasted a root password into the conversation for the test host (identified dashboard-side, deliberately not written here); the repository is public, so the credential is deliberately NOT written anywhere in the repository and should be rotated after the experiment.

D28 was half wrong and is corrected. It asserted that Cloudflare provides NO CLI or API path for connecting a repository to a Worker, so the connection had to be a human-only dashboard step. That is false: Cloudflare documents a Workers Builds REST API (https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/ci-cd/builds/api-reference/, updated 2026-09-22) whose from-scratch example creates the repository connection (PUT /accounts/{id}/builds/repos/connections) and the production and preview triggers (POST /accounts/{id}/builds/triggers) entirely by API. What remains genuinely human-only is narrower and different: the one-time installation and authorization of the Cloudflare GitHub App, which requires an OAuth grant on the GitHub side. The documentation states this explicitly - once that one-time setup is done, the API can do everything else. Credential requirement, measured rather than assumed: the API needs a USER-scoped API token with the Workers Builds Configuration: Edit permission, and the existing wrangler OAuth token is NOT sufficient - GET /accounts/{id}/builds/tokens and GET /builds/repos/connections both returned 403 code 10000 Authentication error on 2026-10-07, while GET /accounts/{id}/workers/scripts succeeded with the same token, which isolates the failure to the Builds permission rather than to authentication in general. Recorded so no future session repeats the claim that the dashboard is the only path, and so the real prerequisite (GitHub App authorization) is not confused with the one that was wrongly claimed.

summary: Q4 is closed and D44 is confirmed by the user. The download mechanism is a Worker-issued short-lived token plus a streamed R2 body, NOT an R2 presigned URL, because a presigned URL cannot be used with a custom domain (verified in D11 / research section 9.2). The user wants a custom domain, a two-hour validity window, and an optional password share. A Worker-issued token delivers all three and is strictly better than presigning on two counts: it is revocable, whereas a presigned URL is an irrevocable bearer token, and it can actually enforce the download-time password check from D15, which a presigned URL bypasses entirely because R2 knows nothing about the password. The accepted cost is that downloads consume this Worker's concurrency and wall-clock budget. With this, every open design question Q1-Q7 is closed and the step-1 grill is complete, so the flow may proceed to step 3, to-spec.

summary: Three requirements added, and they are folded into the spec and the tickets rather than left as conversation. First, authentication becomes self-service: the operator sets a password on first visit and signs in with it thereafter, which REMOVES the earlier plan of issuing a token for the operator to store, and keeps the single-secret architecture because only a salted slow hash is persisted. Ticket 02 was rewritten accordingly and now also requires that changing the password ends existing sessions. Second, sharing becomes explicit: the operator chooses files, sets a lifetime and optionally a password, and the recipient downloads with link plus password; ticket 10 was rewritten and renamed to sharing-links. Third, and largest, DERIVED OBJECTS: the operator wants several stored files combined into one by rule. Running supplied code was considered and rejected in ADR-0003, because this isolate holds every stored machine credential and the master key, so a sandbox escape means every collected machine; the project has already had one temporary diagnostic capability become a live exposure. The transformation is therefore declarative configuration (sources, order, combination, output name), accepting that a transformation the operators cannot express is not possible, with the remedy being to add a bounded operator rather than to open code execution. Tickets 12 and 13 were added: a general merge engine, then structure-aware merging that unions list-valued sections and removes duplicates, which is the actual case (several per-host configuration documents becoming one). A pure-JavaScript YAML parser with no transitive dependencies is available, which matters because anything needing native code or runtime WebAssembly cannot run in this runtime at all.

Tests drive the Worker by calling its own fetch handler, because a plain fetch to a synthetic host does not reach it and fails with Network connection lost. Migration 0003 adds collection_runs, collection_issues, object_flags and object_sources. Two real bugs were found and fixed while doing this, both by tests rather than by inspection. First, the migration splitter removed comments AFTER splitting on semicolons, so a comment containing a semicolon split mid-sentence and its prose was executed as SQL, surfacing as an error naming the word the; it is now extracted to src/sql.ts with seven regression tests. Second, ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN is not repeatable and the second application of the schema failed, which the explicitly-written safe-to-run-again test caught; the fix was a stronger invariant, that migrations use only CREATE, with the importance flag moved into its own table object_flags rather than a new column, and a repo guard scripts/check-migrations.mjs now fails the build if any migration contains an ALTER. The guard was verified both ways: it passes clean and rejects an implanted ALTER. A check about source files was deliberately moved out of the test suite, because the Workers runtime has no filesystem.

operation: implement ticket 02: first-visit password, sessions, sign-out, password change, brute-force limit
reason: Ticket 01 was done, so ticket 02 became the only frontier ticket and is also the highest-risk one: the Worker is publicly reachable and stores real machine credentials with no door on it. Verified before starting that the gap was still open - /api/hosts, /api/rules, /api/usage and /api/status all answered 200 with no credential, and the interface had no sign-in.
expected_start_state: management API and interface fully open; no password concept; 41 tests of which 25 auth tests failing
intended_result: a stranger gets nothing, the operator sets a password on first visit, and the interface has a sign-in gate
after: Implemented and 41/41 tests pass. First visit offers to set a password and the setup path closes itself once one exists, enforced by the row existing rather than a resettable flag. Only a salted PBKDF2 hash at 210k iterations is stored, with the iteration count beside it so the cost can be raised later without invalidating a password. Sessions are HMAC-signed tokens rather than rows, so sign-out and password-change invalidate by moving a timestamp floor instead of deleting anything; both are verified to take effect immediately and every existing session ends on a password change. The signing key is derived from the existing master key, so no second deployment secret was introduced. Failed attempts are recorded and limited per caller. /api/auth/* remains reachable, and /api/admin/apply-schema and /api/status stay public because a fresh deployment has no tables and therefore nowhere to store a password, so the bootstrap must precede the lock; those two expose no credential. TWO REAL BUGS WERE FOUND BY THE TESTS. First, the brute-force counter was global rather than per caller, so one attacker could have locked the operator out entirely - a protection turning into a denial of service against the only account. Second, sessions were issued with second-granularity timestamps while the revocation floor was also seconds, so a token minted in the same second as the floor killed itself; the diagnostic showed issuedAt exactly equal to floor, and the fix was millisecond precision on both sides rather than a tolerance, which keeps revocation strict. Also verified the guard still passes and the build succeeds at 335.62 KiB.
verified_by: pnpm test 41/41; guards pass; wrangler deploy --dry-run exit 0

summary: Ticket 02 is genuinely complete, including three criteria that were unmet when the first commit was made and were finished rather than quietly ticked. Session expiry is now tested by backdating the floor so age is the only reason for refusal, which distinguishes it from the separate floor rule. The non-interactive scheduler credential exists as a credential derived from the master key with its own purpose string, and its distinctness from a session is verified in both directions: a session is refused at the scheduler endpoint and the scheduler credential is refused on the management API. Marking the ticket resolved without these would have been a false claim. While fixing the expiry test, a first attempt was itself wrong: it minted a token before the password existed, so it was refused by the floor rather than by age, which would have passed for the wrong reason.

operation: implement ticket 03: collection rules, and resolving them against a machine
reason: Ticket 03 is the frontier once 01 and 02 are done, and it gates 04 and 05. Its logic existed in the Worker but had no tests at all, which for code that decides which files are ever looked at is the wrong place to have none.
expected_start_state: rule CRUD present but untested; rule resolution inlined in the host-test route against a real SFTP session
intended_result: rules and their resolution covered by tests that run without a machine, with the three-way resolution outcome preserved
after: Extracted a narrow RemoteHost port (src/remote.ts) holding only list/stat/read plus an optional exec for identification, with resolveRules owning the resolution logic. The SSH implementation moved to src/ssh-remote.ts and its API shape was verified against the installed edgeport type declarations rather than assumed: list returns entries with filename and attrs, attrs.size is optional, createReadStream returns a ReadableStream, and run returns a trimmed string. The host-test route now resolves through the port, so rule resolution is driven end to end through the HTTP edge with a substituted remote supplied by the test-only TEST_REMOTE binding, which production never sets. 18 new tests, 65 total, all passing offline. THREE REAL DEFECTS WERE FOUND. First and most important, rulesForHost ordered by is_exclude ASCENDING while claiming in its own comment that exclusions are evaluated first; because the flag is 1 for an exclusion, ascending put inclusions first, which is precisely the ordering that makes an exclusion useless. Caught by a test written for that property. Second, .dev.vars still contained PROBE_HOST, PROBE_USER, PROBE_PORT and PROBE_PASSWORD, credentials for the deleted diagnostic routes; dead configuration pointing at a removed capability is how a removed capability comes back, so it was replaced with the SSH_MASTER_KEY that local development and tests actually need. The new key is git-ignored and verified absent from the tracked tree. Third, tests had been relying on an implicit master-key fallback, so they signed tokens with a different key than the Worker verified with; the key is now stated once in test/fixtures.ts and supplied explicitly, and saving a host with no key set is still refused rather than weakened to make a test pass.
verified_by: pnpm test 65/65; both guards pass; wrangler deploy --dry-run exit 0; edgeport API surface read from its shipped .d.ts
